title: The Glue That Was Too Weak

beats.narration: He made a glue so weak it couldn't hold anything, and his company filed it away as a failure.
It's 1968, and he's a chemist trying to invent a super strong adhesive for building airplanes.
Instead, he gets tiny sticky spheres that peel off anything without leaving a mark.
For years he shows it to anyone who'll listen. "Great, but what's it for?"
Then a coworker who sings in his church choir has a problem: the paper bookmarks keep falling out of his hymn book.
So one Sunday he dabs a little of the weak glue on his bookmarks, and they stay put, then peel right off without tearing a page.
He starts sticking notes on reports for his boss, and the boss writes back on the same little yellow squares.
The first test launch flops, so they hand out free samples in one city, and nine out of ten people order more.
You see, the glue is made of microscopic spheres that only touch the paper at a few points, so it grips just enough to hold and lets go without a fight.

verifiedClaims.text: Spencer Silver at 3M (1968) made a low-tack microsphere adhesive while aiming for a strong one for aircraft.
Art Fry (1974) used it for hymnal bookmarks in his church choir; notes on reports to his boss followed.
The 1977 'Press 'n Peel' test flopped; the 1978 Boise sample blitz had ~90 % reorders; launched 1980.
'Billions sold every year' (tens of billions by many estimates).
